The puzzle omits her particular accomplishment, perhaps deliberately so, as did Sean’s column. She was the first actor who uses a wheelchair to win a Tony. She was cast as Ado Annie in an “Oklahoma” remake which adds an extra layer of depth to “I’m Just a Girl Who Cant’t Say No”.

My English may be good, but there are whole categories of things I'm hopeless with - birds, fish and trees being prime examples. I can name just a few of each, and some of the names don't come with mental images in my head. For example, I know aspen is a some tree, gar is some fish and tern is some bird, but that's it.

Take BUCKEYES - I was only able to type in the final two letters once crosses had given me BUC__YES, and even then the KE there was an educated guess. I looked up the resulting word and learned it's the Polish kasztanowiec, a very popular park tree over here, one I've known all my life - gathering kasztany, buckeye nuts, has been every kid's obsession over here for decades, if not centuries. Still, somehow I've never learned the English name of the tree.

Could somebody please explain the "Monitors for accuracy, just because" clue to me? How does that phrase, specifically, solve to KEEPS HONEST? Why the "just because" part? Clearly I'm not getting something here.

For those who may not know, crossword constructor Sarah Sinclair was a contestant on today’s Jeopardy. Sarah has published several NYT crosswords, including a couple of collaborations with today’s co-creator Rafael Musa. She also did a memorable Thursday grid with Jeopardy champ Paolo Pasco: a puzzle in the shape of a pizza, with rebuses in the crust! Those were the days. (Check out June 27, 2024 in the archive.)

Sadly, Sarah does not get to add Jeopardy champ to her resume, but she was a lot of fun to watch.

Fun and novel! I loved the clues and answers: both were fresh, clever, and funny. Can’t wait until their next crossword collaboration!

I love the tension between the abutting KEEPS HONEST and BENDS THE RULES.  I love seeing SASS close to SMART TVS, as it immediately gets me imagining a TV that talks back to you.

I love seeing EDGY on the border, and SORE next to hurts, and seeing row six – HENS IN POWER – which gets me thinking, “Yes, that might be just what we need.”  Speaking of hens, I love seeing NEST crossing NEST in the SW corner.

These are all serendipities, of course.  What I love most of all today is the feel-good of this puzzle.  Underneath it all is a dedication to fun in wordplay and riddle-cracking and beauty in answer, a dedication toward smoothness and quality.  “Have a good time,” this puzzle says, with ahas and ha-ha’s.

And I did.  This was satisfying, fun, and a hoot.  I came to the box neutral, perked up when I saw your names, Robyn and Rafael, and after solving, left with a bounce to my step.  This was a gift, and a thanks to both of you!

Off-topic re: today's puzzle, but on-topic re: a puzzle a week or two ago. Some may recall that, when ONYCHOPHORAN showed up in a puzzle, someone mentioned me in the comments; I responded, mentioning that when I was a larval biologist, I thought about becoming an "expert" on velvet worms. But then I became totally distracted by... sea slugs. nudibranchs. saccoglossans. There was a great story earlier this week, which I just saw today. It has some great images of nudibranchs in the PNW - many taken in the Salish Sea, where I was based for a while before returning to New England. Sadly, the New England region is depauperate in sea slugs, as with most other intertidal invertebrates. It doesn't show any of the species that I worked on, but you can still get the general idea. And I think you'll understand why I have always been so fascinated by them. FYI, you can see even more abundant diversity in the PNW tide pools, compared to the docks featured in the story. If you click on the link in the story that takes you to the page where the topic of what some sea slugs smell like is discussed, with emphasis on citrus and vanilla, I always thought that Melibe smelled more like pineapple. I'm surprised that wasn't mentioned. https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/27/science/docktober-nudibranchs.html

One more puzzle find. NEVER seen anything else like this. A Thursday from March 29, 2001 by William I. Johnston. Three 'theme' answers. I'll add the clues for those. 20a. "Half of a decoder ring." ABCDEFGHIJKLM 55A. "Other half of the decoder ring." ZYXWVUTSRQPON And then across the middle of the puzzle: "Secret message." LFIXLEVIRHYOLDM And the implication was that those two exchanged letters in the same order, so the implied answer was: OURCOVERISBLOWN Can't imagine having any kind of chance with that one. Here's the link: https://www.xwordinfo.com/Crossword?date=3/29/2001&h=20a .....

Despite being a longtime lurker, this is the first time I felt inspired to comment. This puzzle was an absolute joy. I smiled often during this puzzle's satisfying mix of challenging and clever clues. While some puzzles, with tricky wordplay, will illicit a groan from me, then a begrudging acknowledgment of the clue's cleverness, today's puzzle falls into a more rare & relished category: a tricksy puzzle that delivers nothing but pure delight. 

I wondered why I gravitated to one over the other? Perhaps it is that one puzzle is more adversarial- pitting the setter against the solver, while the other is as if a friend giving you keys to a charming secret. Perhaps it is that I am overthinking it, and it's simply because it's just so dang fun!

My standouts: TRENCHCOAT, DONUTSHOP, AUTOCORRECT

Top billing: WOODSTOVES (still marveling at cords)

This was an inspired partnership and look forward to seeing more in the future! Thank you for joy you brought to my corner of the world, especially since my own supply has been a little short lately.
